title: Write the charter before execution
summary: Agree scope, roles, data, thresholds, and stop conditions.
objectives: Agree scope, roles, data, thresholds, and stop conditions.
Apply pilot charter to the worked customer example and explain its limits.

questions.prompt: A budget field says “to be agreed.” What does that mean for paid cloud execution?

options.rationale: A missing limit is not unlimited permission.

options.text: The budget can be invented after the run.
options.rationale: That prevents an informed decision before spending.

options.text: It is an unresolved prerequisite, not authorization.
options.rationale: The test needs an actual spending agreement before incurring costs.

questions.prompt: A second use case is requested during the pilot. What is the best response?

options.text: Refuse all future discussion of the idea.
options.rationale: It can be a valid next step or an explicit revised scope.

options.text: Document a scope decision and revise criteria, owners, and effort if it is accepted.
options.rationale: The added work has its own evidence and operating requirements.

options.text: Add it silently to look helpful.
options.rationale: That changes the agreed test without informed acceptance.

cards.prompt: What belongs in a pilot charter?
cards.answer: Purpose, scope, data, environment, criteria, roles, limits, stop conditions, and readout.
cards.explanation: These fields make results interpretable and work bounded.

cards.prompt: Why test synthetic edge cases as well as representative inputs?
cards.answer: Rare corrections, duplicates, and failures may not occur in a small real sample.
cards.explanation: Label the evidence basis so synthetic success is not called production proof.

cards.answer: An agreed circumstance that pauses execution or invalidates the comparison.
cards.explanation: It protects the test from continuing under materially changed assumptions.
